<main class="deck">

<section class="panel" id="opening">
<div class="panel-inner">
<div class="kicker"><span class="slide-number">Page 1/3</span> Opening</div>
<h1>BENQODHI</h1>
<p class="subtitle">
From Bengodi to benchmarks
</p>
<p class="main-cue">
AI and quantum computing are often presented as lands of abundance. The point here is to ask for evidence.
</p>

<div class="cue-list">
<div>
<h3>Bengodi</h3>
<p>Boccaccio's imagined land of abundance: parmesan hills, rivers of good wine.</p>
</div>
<div>
<h3>The warning</h3>
<p>Promises of automatic discovery, speedups and solutions to very hard problems need to be tested.</p>
</div>
<div>
<h3>The activity</h3>
<p>Benchmarks, comparison and reproducible tests for AI, quantum, hybrid and classical approaches.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</section>

<section class="panel" id="directions">
<div class="panel-inner">
<div class="kicker"><span class="slide-number">Page 2/3</span> Project directions</div>
<h2>Two complementary directions</h2>
<p class="subtitle">
Controlled theoretical problems on one side; real health and life-science bottlenecks on the other.
</p>

<div class="two-col">
<div>
<h3>Controlled problems</h3>
<p>Two distinct threads: Leiden on quantum algorithms for bioinformatics; La Sapienza on the spin-glass benchmark repository.</p>
<ul>
<li>La Sapienza: controlled theoretical optimization instances</li>
<li>mainly spin-glass-related problems, connected to real complex optimization</li>
<li>used across quantum computing, computer science and physics</li>
<li>needs a shared repository with instances, baselines and comparison rules</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<h3>Health and life sciences</h3>
<p>A scan of real problems that are still computational bottlenecks, where AI, quantum or hybrid methods may become relevant.</p>
<ul>
<li>not only optimization: sampling, inference, reconstruction, simulation and learning</li>
<li>large domains, many kinds of expertise</li>
<li>portfolio approach, also reusing existing benchmarks when useful</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>

<p class="bridge">
The workshop composition matters because the problem is not owned by one field: quantum, optimization, AI, statistical physics, genomics, imaging, medicine, infrastructure and policy all enter the discussion.
</p>
</div>
</section>

<section class="panel" id="workshop">
<div class="panel-inner">
<div class="kicker"><span class="slide-number">Page 3/3</span> Workshop output</div>
<h2>Not a final product: a formulation exercise</h2>
<p class="subtitle">
Tomorrow has two parts: morning round tables, then an afternoon policy session.
</p>

<div class="day-flow">
<div>
<strong>Morning round tables</strong>
<p>Candidate health/life-science problems; benchmark methodology; infrastructure and policy needs.</p>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Afternoon policy session</strong>
<p>Quantum computing technology, resources and policy: short contributions followed by open discussion.</p>
</div>
</div>

<div class="output-grid">
<div>
<strong>Candidate problems</strong>
<p>Which tasks are worth benchmarking?</p>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Existing material</strong>
<p>Which benchmarks or datasets can be reused?</p>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Shared criteria</strong>
<p>What should be measured, compared and reported?</p>
</div>
<div>
<strong>Policy angle</strong>
<p>Which evidence is useful for infrastructure and investment decisions?</p>
</div>
</div>

<p class="closing">
Let us identify good problems, and formulate them well. Solving them can come after.
</p>
</div>
</section>

</main>
